newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland parcel bomb "could have killed".
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland parcel bomb "could have killed".

text.p: A parcel bomb was sent to a prominent Protestant politician on Thursday in a grim reminder of the fragility of efforts to bring peace to Northern Ireland.
The device sent to Robert McCartney, leader of the small pro-British UK Unionist Party, was "crude but viable" and could have caused injury, police said. It was made safe by army experts.
McCartney, who is on holiday abroad, said the bomb could have proved fatal.
"The parcel, if opened, would probably have been fatal, or at the very least would have caused very disfiguring injuries," he told BBC radio.

McCartney said he had opposed the activities of both Irish republican and pro-British "loyalist" guerrillas and he was in the dark as to who might have sent the bomb, which was packed with explosives and ball-bearings.
The UK Unionists have walked out of the current round of peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland.

Adam Ingram, the Northern Ireland security minister, said the parcel bomb was a matter of regret although he did not think it represented a breach of the ceasefire declared at the weekend by the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

Some 3,200 people have been killed in the past three decades of conflict between Protestants and Roman Catholics in Northern Ireland. The British and Irish governments are struggling to keep peace efforts on track after Protestant politicians rejected key proposals on the surrender of guerrilla arms.

"It's clearly a setback, but I don't think it's a long-lasting setback," former U.S. senator George Mitchell, chairman of the province's peace talks, told reporters after Protestant unionist parties voted the plan down.
Belfast newspapers said Wednesday's vote cast doubts over the future of the talks process, but the Dublin media applauded Anglo-Irish determination to press ahead with negotiations.
"Further delay will kill the talks," said Belfast's nationalist Irish News, while the News Letter, read by unionists, asked: "Where do we go now?"
The Irish Times, published in Dublin, said the main Ulster Unionist Party may have disrupted the talks timetable but they must know that "the settlement train will not be derailed".
Meanwhile Northern Ireland police said they had found bomb-making equipment in a roadside ditch.
About eight kg (18 lbs) of explosives and eight coffee jars adapted to be used as bombs had been seized in the find at Pomeroy, County Tyrone on Wednesday.
The IRA has stockpiles of arms and explosives concealed in Northern Ireland and the Irish republic.
The unionist vote on Wednesday dashed hopes of a compromise on the surrender of guerrilla weapons after 14 months of deadlock and painstaking Anglo-Irish diplomacy.
The unionists rejected the plan because it would have allowed the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to take part in talks without surrendering any of its guns and bombs.

The IRA ordered a truce last weekend in its 28-year war against British rule, but unionists tended to dismiss it as a ploy to enable Sinn Fein to attend substantive peace negotiations due to start on September 15.

Two small unionist parties, the Democratic Unionists and the UK Unionists, walked out of the talks after the vote and the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party insisted that it would not negotiate with Sinn Fein while its IRA allies remain armed.
